captions.text: Picture a June evening in the south of Sweden, more than half a century ago.
A tractor is coming home from the fields.
It hardly drinks any diesel: it eats wood!
Let’s follow one small wood chip.
It waits in the dry of the barn, among thousands of sisters.
It was born under the knives of a chipper.
Now here it is on the tractor, which carries it off to the field.
It rides on the roof rack, before dropping into the bunker.
Its journey begins.
It sinks, gently: about an hour.
It dries.
It blackens and falls apart.
It passes under a flame: a fire short of air, on purpose.
Then, in a bed of red-hot charcoal, the gas cools…
and becomes fuel!
At the bottom, almost nothing is left.
The gas carries on, still very hot: it crosses a filter, then a cooler.
In the cylinder, a thread of diesel lights it.
On the test bench, a Swedish institute counted two hundred and twenty-one kilowatts going in for forty at the shaft.
Eighteen per cent.
And then, one evening, the engine stops.
But the gas does not stop with it.
This is the gravest story in this lab.
First, a few pointers.
There are five worlds, from the farm to the garage.
Click a part: its sheet opens, and you can listen to its story.
Assembly tells, in the past tense, how the system went together: a reading, not a procedure.
Installation says what had to be gathered before the first day.
The simulation lets you change the load and the moisture of the wood.
Seven lessons explain the physics.
Ten drawings sketch it.
One last thing: this laboratory is an independent educational reconstruction.
It is neither an official design nor a maker’s product.
It explains a machine from history, and gives no plans.
The published figures come from that institute’s report and from a Swedish book on the gasifiers of the war.
The others come out of the simulation.
On the sheets, a figure with no mark is published; a cross marks a calculation, a star an estimate.
The Sources panel says who said what.
Take your time: a chip takes an hour to come down.
A large farm in the south of Sweden, around nineteen seventy.
The wood begins here, in the dry of the barn.
The chipper cuts it into small chips, and the sieve rids them of their fines.
The tractor carries them off, and drags a four-metre clod crusher behind it.
What the machine leaves behind, the ash, and some black water, ends up in a bin and in a barrel.
And there, built against the house, the garage.
Keep it in mind.
The farm has no source: its walls are drawn to the scale of a five-tonne tractor.
What is real is what the machine did there: more than two thousand five hundred hours in six years.
The machine, on paper, rolling on the spot.
An ordinary tractor, and on its left flank, the gasifier: four hundred and fifty kilos more.
Its top almost reaches the driver’s eye.
Watch the cab fade away!
On the roof, a rack carries the day’s chips.
And the gas runs to the engine, through a filter and a cooler.
Let’s pull the parts apart a little, to see what carries what…
Nothing floats: every part has its support.

segments.title: The journey of a wood chip

captions.text: Here is the apparatus, always in section, and its travelling chip.
It goes in through the lid, and there, the column draws it gently downwards: about an hour.
First it dries: the water vapour escapes.
Then it breaks down into charcoal and vapours.
Those vapours must cross the flame.
After that the hot gas crosses red-hot charcoal, where it cools: that is where it becomes fuel.
A little ash is left: that is the end of the journey.
The zones are in order, not to scale: on purpose.

The wood going in, the gas, the diesel, the work at the shaft, and in grey, the losses.
